    United States Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court
    Established: October 25, 1978
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of 1978 is a U.S. federal law establishing procedures for physical and electronic surveillance of foreign intelligence on domestic soil. It established the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) to oversee warrant requests, primarily targeting foreign powers and agents. Section 702 is a major, contentious provision allowing warrantless targeting of non-U.S. persons outside the U.S., which often captures Americans' data, sparking intense reauthorization debates. 
    Key Aspects of FISA 
    • Purpose: Enacted to prevent illegal warrantless surveillance of Americans, it authorizes, limits, and regulates surveillance for foreign intelligence gathering.
    • Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC): A specialized court established to review and approve applications for surveillance warrants, physical searches, and, under Section 702, targeting procedures.
    • Section 702: Allows for the targeting of non-U.S. persons located outside the U.S. to gather foreign intelligence, often involving US electronic communication service providers.
    • Targeting Requirements: Unlike regular warrants, Section 702 does not require an individual warrant for each target; instead, it relies on court-approved targeting and minimization procedures, as detailed on Intelligence.gov.
    • Controversy and Reform: FISA has been amended over time (e.g., in 2008), with concerns focusing on "incidental" collection of American communications and potential misuse of data by federal agencies. 
    Current Status and Reauthorization
    As of April 2026, Congress is debating the reauthorization of Section 702, which is set to expire on April 20. Debates are focused on implementing new safeguards for Americans' privacy while maintaining its usefulness for national security, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. Some lawmakers are proposing attaching, for example, the Save America Act, which would add, for instance, a requirement of proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections and the presentation of an ID to cast a ballot.
